glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Solomon calls worshipers to listen, keep their vows, and fear God, then shows that the love of money and lost riches leave a person empty-handed, and names the power to enjoy food, work, and wealth as the gift of God.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Chapter 5 sits at the center of Ecclesiastes 4:1–6:12, Solomon’s look at life in society. After the oppression and fading fame of chapter 4, he turns from observing to commanding, starting in “the house of God,” most likely the temple in Jerusalem.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “As for every man to whom God has given riches and wealth, and given him power to eat of it, to receive his heritage and rejoice in his labor—this is the gift of God.” (Ecclesiastes 5:19)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Ecclesiastes 5 opens with a sudden change of voice. Through chapter 4 Solomon has been watching: the tears of the oppressed, envious work, lonely toil. Now he speaks directly to his hearers, and the first place he takes them is God’s house. There he tells them to “draw near to hear rather than to give the sacrifice of fools.” Worshipers who pour out sacrifices and words without listening do wrong without even knowing it. “For God is in heaven, and you on earth; Therefore let your words be few.” God’s greatness does not keep the worshiper away. It makes every word, and especially every vow, weigh something before Him. Solomon gathers the whole counsel into three words, “But fear God,” which call for a right view of who God is.

From there the chapter moves out into the province and the marketplace, and from verse 8 through verse 17 God is not named. This suggests what life looks like when it is measured only by officials, silver, and labor: it ends in empty hands. The rich man returns to the grave “naked,” and Solomon asks the book’s opening question again: “what profit has he who has labored for the wind?” Then God comes back into view as the Giver. The same ordinary act describes both lives. The man who labored for the wind “eats in darkness” all his days, while the one who receives from God eats and drinks “all the days of his life which God gives him.” What separates them is whether they receive their days, their goods, and even the power to enjoy them from His hand.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Ecclesiastes 5:1–3 — Drawing Near to Hear in the House of God

Solomon tells worshipers to come to God’s house ready to listen, because offerings from people who will not listen are “the sacrifice of fools.” Since God is in heaven and they are on earth, their words before Him should be few and weighed, and a proverb about dreams and much activity shows that a flood of words gives away the fool.

Ecclesiastes 5:4–7 — Paying What You Vow to God

No one had to make a vow, but once a vow was made to God it had to be paid without delay, for it is “Better not to vow than to vow and not pay.” Calling a broken promise “an error” before the messenger of God does not escape God Himself, and Solomon sums up all of verses 1–7 with the command “But fear God.”

Ecclesiastes 5:8–9 — Oppression Among Layers of Officials

Solomon tells his hearers not to be astonished when the poor are oppressed and justice is twisted in a province, because “high official watches over high official.” Whether those officials are checking one another or protecting one another, higher authority is no guarantee of justice; being unsurprised by oppression is not the same as approving it, and beneath the whole chain of power lies the land, for “even the king is served from the field.”

Ecclesiastes 5:10–12 — The Love of Money Never Satisfies

“He who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver”: the trouble lies in loving money, and that desire can never be filled. As goods increase, so do the people who consume them, and the rich man’s abundance often costs him the sweet sleep that the laboring man enjoys.

Ecclesiastes 5:13–17 — Riches Lost and Nothing Carried Away

With the formal words “There is a severe evil which I have seen under the sun,” Solomon describes riches hoarded to their owner’s harm, lost through misfortune, and leaving nothing for his son. Every person leaves this world as naked as he entered it, carrying nothing from his labor, and the man who “labored for the wind” spends even his present days in darkness, sorrow, and anger.

Ecclesiastes 5:18–20 — Enjoyment as the Gift of God

Against that emptiness Solomon commends eating, drinking, and enjoying one’s work as one’s “heritage,” and he calls both wealth and the power to enjoy it “the gift of God.” Joy from God keeps a person from being consumed by how brief life is, without asking him to pretend hardship is unreal, because “God keeps him busy with the joy of his heart.”

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Ecclesiastes 5 shows that worship begins with listening and truthful speech. God invites His people to draw near, yet because He is in heaven He takes their words seriously, and a promise made to Him cannot be brushed aside as a mistake.

The chapter also explains why money cannot satisfy. Wealth multiplies claims and worries, and death takes all of it away. The thirst Solomon exposes in verse 10 is met, in the wider witness of Scripture, by Christ, who offers water that ends thirst (John 4:13–14).

Finally, the chapter separates having from enjoying. Possessions and the power to enjoy them are both gifts from God, so wealth is neither evil in itself nor proof of His approval, and contentment rests on knowing the generous Giver. Chapter 6 opens with a man who has riches without that second gift (6:1–2).

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Reverent listening and honest words. Worship starts with hearing God, and words spoken before Him, especially vows, carry real weight (5:1–7).

Injustice among layers of authority. Solomon expects oppression in public life and refuses to treat higher officials as a guarantee of justice, without excusing the wrong (5:8–9; see 4:1).

The restless love of money. Desire for wealth grows with every increase and robs its lover of rest (5:10–12; compare 1:8; 4:8).

Empty hands at death. Hoarded riches can vanish, no one carries anything out of this world, and the book’s opening question about profit returns (5:13–17; see 1:3).

Enjoyment as the gift of God. Food, work, wealth, and the ability to enjoy them are received from God as a person’s heritage (5:18–20; see 6:1–2).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
The house of God (5:1). Most likely the temple in Jerusalem, where Israel brought sacrifices and paid vows.

Vow (5:4–6). A voluntary promise made to God. No one had to vow, but a vow once made was binding. Solomon’s point is honesty before God; he is not commending a promise that would require doing what God forbids.

The messenger of God (5:6). Most likely a priest or another temple representative who received the vow; Malachi 2:7 describes the priest as God’s messenger. Some understand an angel instead. Either way, the excuse cannot escape God.

Fear God (5:7). A right view of God that shows itself in reverence, worship, trust, and obedience. Here it sums up the whole call to listen and to keep one’s word.

Vanity (5:7, 10). The NKJV word for a Hebrew term that pictures a breath or vapor, something that cannot be held. In Ecclesiastes it means meaningless: empty and futile when life is pursued without God. In verse 7 it describes piled-up dreams and words; in verse 10, the endless chase after more.

Heritage and the gift of God (5:18–19). A person’s God-given portion in life. In verse 19 both the riches and the “power to eat of it” come from God, so having and enjoying are two separate gifts.

focus: Ecclesiastes 5 brings Solomon’s survey of life in society into the house of God, where he calls for attentive listening, honest vows, and the fear of God. Turning back to the province and the marketplace, he shows that oppression, the love of money, and the loss of riches leave a person with nothing to carry away, and he closes by setting against that empty pursuit the gift of God: the power to enjoy food, work, and wealth as one’s heritage from His hand.

sections.title: Drawing Near to Hear in the House of God
sections.summary: Solomon tells the worshiper to come to God’s house ready to listen rather than to offer “the sacrifice of fools,” and to keep speech few, “For God is in heaven, and you on earth.” A proverb about dreams and many words shows that a flood of words reveals the fool.

sections.title: Paying What You Vow to God
sections.summary: A vow made to God must be paid without delay, for it is “Better not to vow than to vow and not pay.” Solomon warns against excusing a broken promise before the messenger of God as a mistake, and he gathers the whole call to worship into one command: “But fear God.”

sections.title: Oppression Among Layers of Officials
sections.summary: Solomon tells his hearers not to be astonished when they see the poor oppressed and justice twisted in a province, because “high official watches over high official” within a chain of authority. Yet the produce of the land sustains everyone, and “even the king is served from the field.”

sections.title: The Love of Money Never Satisfies
sections.summary: “He who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver.” More goods only bring more people to consume them, and while “The sleep of a laboring man is sweet,” the rich man’s abundance keeps him awake.

sections.title: Riches Lost and Nothing Carried Away
sections.summary: Solomon describes a “severe evil”: riches hoarded to the owner’s harm, lost through misfortune, and leaving nothing for his son. Everyone leaves this world as he entered it, “naked,” taking nothing from his labor, and the man who “labored for the wind” spends his days in darkness, sorrow, and anger.

sections.title: Enjoyment as the Gift of God
sections.summary: Against that emptiness Solomon commends eating, drinking, and enjoying one’s labor as one’s heritage, and he calls both wealth and the power to enjoy it “the gift of God.” The person who receives these gifts is not consumed by the brevity of life, because “God keeps him busy with the joy of his heart.”

1.brief: Solomon turns from watching life in society to giving direct instruction: whoever goes to “the house of God” must come carefully, ready to listen. Offerings from people who will not listen to God are “the sacrifice of fools,” and such worshipers do wrong without even realizing it.
1.explain:
Walk prudently when you go to the house of God opens the chapter with a sudden change of voice. Through chapter 4 Solomon has been observing life in society: the tears of the oppressed, work driven by envy, lonely toil, and popular favor that fades. Now he speaks directly to his hearers, and the first place he takes them is God’s house, most likely the temple in Jerusalem, where Israel brought its sacrifices and paid its vows. To walk prudently is to watch one’s steps and come carefully, aware of where one is going and before whom one will stand. These commands are plain, positive instruction within the book. They are not one more conclusion of the search that Solomon exposes as empty.

and draw near to hear shows what coming carefully looks like. The worshiper is not told to stay away. God’s house is a place to draw near, but the purpose of coming is to listen. Listening comes first because the worshiper comes to receive from God, not to impress Him, and a person who truly hears what God says is ready to respond to it.

rather than to give the sacrifice of fools sets that listening against a different kind of worship. Sacrifices were part of the worship God gave Israel, so the problem is not the offering itself but the person offering it. In Ecclesiastes, as in Proverbs, the fool is someone who will not heed wisdom. Here the fool brings a gift to God with no intention of listening to Him. The offering becomes a substitute for attention, as if giving something could take the place of hearing.

for they do not know that they do evil explains why this matters so much. These worshipers think they are doing something good. They go through the motions of devotion and leave satisfied, never realizing that careless worship is itself wrong. Their blindness to their own fault is part of their folly. That blindness is why Solomon begins with a warning instead of assuming that everyone who comes to God’s house comes rightly.
1.notes:
Printed Hebrew Bibles count this verse as the last verse of chapter 4 (4:17). Hebrew chapter 5 therefore begins with the verse English Bibles number 5:2, and it has one fewer verse. The English division, followed by both the NKJV and NLT, keeps the call to “draw near to hear” together with the counsel about speech that it introduces in verses 2–3.

The NLT paraphrases this verse as “keep your ears open and your mouth shut” and calls the fools’ sacrifices “mindless offerings.” Its wording brings forward the contrast between listening and speaking that verse 2 develops, and it interprets the folly as worship offered without thought. The NKJV keeps the separate images of walking and drawing near, which the NLT combines in “As you enter.”

2.brief: Because “God is in heaven, and you on earth,” the worshiper must not rush into rash words or hasty promises before Him, and so “let your words be few.” This humility does not mean God is distant or unwilling to hear. It means that words spoken to Him carry real weight and should be measured.
2.explain:
Do not be rash with your mouth moves from coming to God’s house to speaking there. Rash words are words that run ahead of thought. In the setting of worship they include hasty prayers, careless claims, and especially promises made to God on impulse, which verses 4–6 address directly.

And let not your heart utter anything hastily before God carries the warning inward. The mouth speaks, but the heart is where words begin, so Solomon addresses both the spoken words and the inner impulse behind them. The words “before God” show why haste is so dangerous here: the worshiper is speaking in God’s presence, not into empty air.

For God is in heaven, and you on earth gives the reason. God rules over all from heaven, while the worshiper is a creature standing on the earth He made. That difference calls for humility and accountability. It does not mean that God is far away or unwilling to listen. This same verse assumes the worshiper will speak to Him, and the previous verse tells the worshiper to draw near. God’s greatness is what gives weight to every word spoken to Him. Ecclesiastes calls this reverence the fear of God, which is a right view of who He is.

Therefore let your words be few draws the conclusion. Because words spoken before God carry real weight, they should be measured and meant. Solomon is not setting a numerical limit on prayer. He is warning against piling up words without thought, as though many words could impress God or make up for not listening.
2.notes: The NLT renders the first line “Don’t make rash promises” and the second “don’t be hasty in bringing matters before God.” This wording points ahead to the vows of verses 4–6. The NKJV’s “rash with your mouth” and “utter anything hastily” are broader and cover any careless speech before God. That broader wording fits the structure of the passage: verses 1–3 concern listening and restrained speech in general, and verses 4–7 narrow the subject to the vow.

3.brief: A proverb backs up the call for few words: just as a busy, restless life produces dreams, so a flood of words gives away the fool. The comparison exposes restless activity and careless talk; it is not a statement about every dream.
3.explain:
For a dream comes through much activity begins a short proverb that supports the call for few words, and the opening “For” ties it to verse 2. “Much activity” describes a crowded life full of effort and concern, and dreams are what such a life produces at night. The line draws on ordinary experience: a restless day leads to restless sleep. Solomon uses this as a comparison. It is not a teaching about the meaning or source of every dream, and it says nothing against God’s ability to speak to His people.

And a fool’s voice is known by his many words completes the comparison. Just as busy days produce dreams, a fool produces a flood of words, and that flood gives him away. His voice is “known,” recognized for what it is, by how much he talks. In the setting of worship, the proverb explains why few words are wise in God’s presence. A stream of careless talk is no proof of devotion. Instead, it shows a person who has not stopped to listen.
3.notes:
Verse 7 deliberately echoes this verse: “For in the multitude of dreams and many words there is also vanity. But fear God.” Because dreams and many words appear together in both verses, verses 1–7 hold together as one unit, and the closing command “But fear God” sums up the whole passage on worship and vows.

The NLT renders the second line “too many words make you a fool,” which suggests that excessive talk produces foolishness. The NKJV’s “a fool’s voice is known by his many words” presents many words as the evidence that reveals a fool who is already there. Both renderings support the proverb’s warning, but the NKJV keeps the focus on recognition.

Later in the book Solomon makes a similar observation about ordinary speech: “A fool also multiplies words” (10:14). Too many words mark the fool in worship and in daily life alike.

The general purpose of the dream comparison is clear, but its precise force is less certain. The line may stress that anxious busyness leads to restless dreams. It may also point more broadly to activity that, like many words, produces little of substance, a reading supported by the link verse 7 draws between many dreams and vanity. Either way, the comparison supports the call for few words before God.

4.brief: Solomon moves from speech in general to one specific kind of speech, the vow, and says that a promise made to God must be kept without delay. God takes no pleasure in fools who promise and then put off keeping their word, so the verse presses the plain command, “Pay what you have vowed.”
4.explain:
When you make a vow to God, do not delay to pay it — Solomon now narrows the counsel of verses 1–3. He has warned against rash speech before God in general; here he takes up one specific kind of speech, the vow. A vow was a voluntary promise made to God, and Israel brought sacrifices and paid vows at the house of God, most likely the temple in Jerusalem. The word “When” assumes that worshipers will sometimes make vows, and Solomon does not forbid them. His command concerns timing. A vow that is put off again and again is broken by degrees: the person keeps speaking as though payment is coming while holding on to what was promised.

For He has no pleasure in fools — This is the reason for the command. The fool in this verse is the person who makes a promise to God and then delays keeping it. God takes no delight in words offered to Him that are never matched by action, however sincere or impressive they sounded when they were spoken. What pleases Him is a worshiper whose word to Him can be trusted.

Pay what you have vowed — Solomon repeats the duty as a plain, unqualified command. Once a vow is spoken it is owed to God, so paying it simply gives Him what was promised. Solomon’s concern is honesty before God; he is not commending a promise that would require doing what God forbids.
4.notes:
The NKJV ends this verse with a dash after “Pay what you have vowed,” so the command runs directly into the comparison of verse 5. The punctuation presents the two verses as one connected thought: pay the vow, because it is better never to vow than to leave a vow unpaid.

The word “fools” ties this verse to “the sacrifice of fools” in verse 1 and to “a fool’s voice” in verse 3. In all three verses the fool is marked by careless worship or speech before God, so the warning about vows continues the same portrait instead of opening a new subject.

5.brief: No one had to make a vow, but once made, a vow was binding. That is why it is “Better not to vow than to vow and not pay”: staying silent is wiser than promising God something and then failing to give it.
5.explain:
Better not to vow than to vow and not pay — The whole verse is a single comparison. No one in Israel was required to make a vow, so choosing not to vow was no failure before God. Once a vow was spoken, however, it was binding, and leaving it unpaid was a real wrong. Silence is therefore the wiser course than a promise that will not be kept.

This saying applies the warning of verse 2, “let not your heart utter anything hastily before God,” to the vow in particular. The verse does not discourage generous devotion to God. It discourages promises made in a moment of feeling without weighing whether they can be kept. A worshiper who stays silent has said nothing false before God, while one who vows and fails to pay has spoken a promise that proved untrue.
5.notes: This verse weighs two options in the same way as several sayings of the previous chapter: “Better a handful with quietness Than both hands full” (4:6), “Two are better than one” (4:9), and “Better a poor and wise youth Than an old and foolish king” (4:13). Each saying sets two possibilities side by side and names the wiser one. Here the two possibilities are silence and an unpaid vow.

6.brief: Solomon warns against letting careless words draw the whole person into sin, first by making a vow and then by telling “the messenger of God” that it was only “an error.” This messenger was most likely a priest or another temple representative (some understand an angel). Either way, the excuse cannot escape God, who may be angered by it and bring “the work of your hands” to nothing.
6.explain:
Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin — The mouth is one small part of a person, yet careless words can bring the whole person into guilt. “Flesh” here refers to the person in ordinary bodily life, the one who must live with what the mouth has promised. A rash vow is the first step in that direction, because words spoken in a moment commit the whole life that follows.

nor say before the messenger of God that it was an error — The second step is the attempted escape. Having vowed and failed to pay, the worshiper tells the messenger of God that the vow was a mistake. This messenger was most likely a priest or another temple representative who received or oversaw the vow, since the whole passage is set at the house of God and concerns vows brought there. Malachi 2:7 calls the priest God’s messenger, which supports this reading, though this verse does not name the office. Some interpreters understand an angel instead. Either way, the excuse is spoken in God’s presence. Calling a deliberate promise “an error” treats it as an innocent slip, and the next clause names that claim for what it is: an excuse.

Why should God be angry at your excuse and destroy the work of your hands? — Solomon closes with a question meant to stop the worshiper short. Why provoke God? The verse places His anger on the excuse itself, the attempt to talk one’s way out of an accountable promise. “The work of your hands” means the labor and achievements of a person’s life. Someone who holds back what was promised in order to protect possessions is shortsighted, because God can bring all that work to nothing. The question warns of what God may do; it does not turn every setback in a person’s work into proof of a broken vow.
6.notes:
The Hebrew word translated “messenger” covers a wide range. It can describe any person sent to carry a message or act on someone else’s behalf, including a person sent on God’s behalf, and it is also the word the Old Testament uses for angels. The word by itself therefore cannot settle who is meant here. The identification depends on the setting of the verse.

The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament presents the excuse as spoken before God Himself. That wording stresses the worshiper’s accountability to God, but it does not by itself show whether the messenger in the Hebrew text is a priest.

The NLT translates the phrase as “the Temple messenger,” which builds the human, temple-based reading into the translation itself. The NKJV’s “the messenger of God” keeps the wording open, so the identification remains an interpretation of the phrase and not something the text states outright.

7.brief: Echoing the dreams and many words of verse 3, Solomon sums up the whole passage: piling up dreams and words is meaningless, empty activity that achieves nothing before God. Against all of it he sets one command, “But fear God,” which calls the worshiper to a right view of God that shows itself in listening and in honest promises.
7.explain:
For in the multitude of dreams and many words there is also vanity — Solomon returns to the two images of verse 3, where “a dream comes through much activity” and “a fool’s voice is known by his many words.” Bringing them back here gathers up the whole passage that began in verse 1. “Vanity” is the NKJV word for a Hebrew term that pictures a breath or vapor, something that cannot be held, and in Ecclesiastes it means meaningless. Dreams and words piled up before God are empty in that sense: they produce activity and sound but leave nothing of substance. As in verse 3, the comparison exposes restless activity and careless speech; it is not a statement about every dream.

But fear God — Against all that empty talk Solomon sets one short command. To fear God is to have a right view of Him, a view that shows itself in reverence, worship, trust, and obedience. In this passage that right view takes specific forms: drawing near to hear (verse 1), keeping words few because “God is in heaven, and you on earth” (verse 2), and paying what has been vowed (verses 4–6). A worshiper who truly sees who God is will listen before speaking and will keep the promises made to Him.
7.notes:
Translations handle this verse differently. The NKJV keeps the pairing of dreams and many words from verse 3, while the NLT paraphrases more freely: “Talk is cheap, like daydreams and other useless activities.” Both renderings make the same basic point, that multiplied words and dreams are empty before God, although the precise force of the dream comparison is less certain than that main point.

The command “But fear God” is the first time Ecclesiastes directly tells the reader to fear God. Other passages describe the fear of God (3:14; 7:18; 8:12–13), but the only other direct command is the book’s conclusion: “Fear God and keep His commandments” (12:13).

8.brief: Turning to public life, Solomon tells his hearers not to be astonished when they see the poor oppressed and justice violently twisted in a province. His reason is that “high official watches over high official, and higher officials are over them.” Those layered officials may be checking one another or protecting one another's interests, but in either case higher authority is no guarantee of justice for the poor, and not being surprised by oppression does not mean accepting it as right.
8.explain:
If you see the oppression of the poor — Solomon leaves the house of God and turns to public life, but he keeps speaking directly to his hearer, just as he did in verses 1–7. The word “if” does not suggest that oppression is rare. It pictures an ordinary observer coming across something that happens often enough to be seen. The victims are “the poor,” the people with the least money and the least power to defend themselves. Solomon has looked at this before. In 4:1 he considered “all the oppression that is done under the sun” and saw the tears of the oppressed, who had no comforter while power stood on the side of those who oppressed them.

and the violent perversion of justice and righteousness — The second scene concerns justice itself. A perversion is something twisted out of its proper form, and “violent” adds force: justice is bent deliberately and under pressure. “Justice and righteousness” belong together here, describing both the fair decision that should protect the weak and the right dealing that should mark the whole community. The very things meant to shelter the poor have become the means of wronging them. Solomon has seen this too, for in 3:16 he observed that “In the place of judgment, Wickedness was there.”

in a province — A province is a governed district with officials and administration. The injustice Solomon describes does not happen on a lawless frontier where no one is in charge. It happens inside an organized system of government, and that is exactly why the verse goes on to speak about the officials themselves.

do not marvel at the matter — Solomon tells his hearer not to be astonished. He is preparing the reader for what life in a fallen world actually looks like, so that the sight of oppression does not leave him shaken as though something unheard of had happened. Not being surprised is different from approving. Nothing in the verse calls the oppression right or tells the hearer to stop caring about the poor. What it removes is the naive expectation that a system of authority will automatically produce fair results.

for high official watches over high official, and higher officials are over them — Here Solomon gives his reason. Officials stand in layers, each beneath another, with still higher officials above them all. “Watches over” can describe supervision, with each level keeping an eye on the one below it. It can also describe officials watching out for one another and protecting a shared interest. The verse does not settle which picture is in view, and in either case the poor stand at the bottom of the chain. Each added layer can mean one more official taking a share or one more official looking away, so higher authority offers no guarantee that justice will reach the people who need it. The verse does not promise that a superior will step in and put things right, and it does not identify the highest authority as God. Solomon has already declared that “God shall judge the righteous and the wicked” (3:17), but in this verse he describes the chain of human power as an observer sees it under the sun.
8.notes:
The NLT renders the second half of the verse, “For every official is under orders from higher up, and matters of justice get lost in red tape and bureaucracy.” That translation reads the chain of officials as a system in which responsibility is passed upward and justice is delayed until it disappears. The NKJV’s “high official watches over high official” is less specific and leaves room for either oversight or mutual protection among the officials. The precise way the hierarchy operates is debated.

The NKJV word “province” appears in the plural in 2:8, where Solomon gathered “the special treasures of kings and of the provinces.” In both places the word belongs to the world of royal administration that Solomon knew from the throne. The NLT’s “throughout the land” in 5:8 is more general and does not keep that administrative picture.

9.brief: Beneath the whole chain of officials lies the land itself, whose produce sustains everyone in society. The wording of this verse is difficult and should not be pressed into a theory of government, but its plain point is that “even the king is served from the field.”
9.explain:
Moreover the profit of the land is for all — With “Moreover” Solomon adds a further observation to what he has just said about the officials. “Profit” is a key word in Ecclesiastes for the gain left over from labor, the very thing the book’s opening question asks about (1:3). Here the profit is the produce of the land, the harvest that the fields yield, and that produce benefits everyone in society. Beneath the whole chain of officials in verse 8 lies the soil, and every layer of that hierarchy lives on what the land brings forth.

even the king is served from the field — The word “even” points to the top of the chain. The king, the highest human authority over every official, still depends on the field for his food. The verse does not draw out every implication, but placed beside verse 8 it shows that the ruler who sits above all the officials is sustained by land that ordinary people work, the same people who stand at the bottom of the chain. Because the wording of this verse is difficult, its details should not carry a theory of government. Its plain point is enough: all human power, however high it rises, rests on the provision of the field.
9.notes:
Translations handle this verse quite differently. The NLT reads, “Even the king milks the land for his own profit!” That rendering ties verse 9 to the oppression of verse 8 by making the king one more beneficiary at the land’s expense. The NKJV presents the land’s produce as benefiting everyone, with the king served from the field like the rest of society. The difference reflects the difficulty of the verse’s wording.

Verse 9 introduces the word “profit,” which returns twice in the verses that follow: “what profit have the owners” (5:11) and “what profit has he who has labored for the wind?” (5:16). The repeated word links this short observation about the land to the teaching on wealth that comes next, even though the subject of verses 8–9 is injustice in public life rather than private riches.

God is not named from verse 8 through verse 17. After the command “But fear God” (5:7), He is not mentioned again until verse 18, where Solomon speaks of the days of life “which God gives him.” The officials, the land, and the king of verses 8–9 belong to the stretch of the chapter in which life is described without reference to Him.

10.brief: Solomon now turns to private wealth: the one who loves money is never satisfied by money, and the one who loves abundance never finds enough in more. The problem is the love of money, not money itself, and because that desire can never be filled, “This also is vanity”: chasing wealth for satisfaction is meaningless.
10.explain:
He who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver moves Solomon’s attention from injustice in the province (verses 8–9) to the private pursuit of wealth. Silver stands for money here, which is why the NLT simply says “money.” Notice how Solomon describes this man. He does not say the man has too little. He names what the man loves, and the thing he loves is the very thing that cannot fill him. Each gain sharpens the appetite instead of ending it. So the trouble lies in loving money, not in money itself. Later in this chapter Solomon calls riches and wealth “the gift of God” (verse 19).

Nor he who loves abundance, with increase repeats the thought in wider terms. “Abundance” reaches beyond coins to possessions of every kind, and “increase” is the growth the lover of abundance keeps hoping will finally be enough. The second line rules out the idea that some other form of wealth will succeed where silver failed. Whatever form the abundance takes, having more of it does not bring rest.

This also is vanity gives Solomon’s verdict. The Hebrew word the NKJV translates “vanity” pictures a breath or vapor, something that cannot be held. In Ecclesiastes it marks a pursuit as meaningless when life is pursued without God. The word “also” places the love of money beside the other pursuits Solomon has already tested and found empty. God is not named from verse 8 through verse 17, and the verdict fits that silence: when silver is loved as the source of satisfaction, the search for enough never ends. In the wider witness of Scripture, the thirst this verse exposes is met by Christ, who offers water that ends thirst (John 4:13–14).
10.notes:
The NLT expands the short verdict “This also is vanity” into an explanation: “How meaningless to think that wealth brings true happiness!” That rendering states openly what the NKJV leaves implied: the futile thing is expecting wealth to satisfy.

This complaint belongs to a thread that runs through this part of the book. In 4:8 the lonely worker labors without end, “Nor is his eye satisfied with riches,” and in 6:7 Solomon observes that “All the labor of man is for his mouth, And yet the soul is not satisfied.”

11.brief: As goods increase, so does the number of people who live off them: household, servants, and everyone else with a claim on the wealth. What grows also flows out to others, so the owner's only real “profit” is to look at what he has.
11.explain:
When goods increase, They increase who eat them describes what happens as wealth grows. The number of people who live from it grows too: household members, servants, workers, and everyone else with a claim on the estate. “Eat” is plain language for consumption. The goods are used up by mouths other than the owner’s, so growing possessions do not pile up in one place. They flow out to others almost as fast as they come in.

So what profit have the owners raises the question that runs through the whole book. “Profit” is the lasting gain left after labor, the very thing asked about in 1:3. The word appeared just before this in verse 9, where “the profit of the land is for all.” Now Solomon asks the question about the wealthy themselves: if the people around them consume the increase, what is actually left for the owners?

Except to see them with their eyes? gives the answer with quiet irony. The owner’s one remaining benefit is the sight of his goods. He can look at what he has, but he cannot stop the stream of people who consume it, and looking is a thin return for so much effort. The verse does not condemn owning goods or providing for a household. It shows how little the lover of abundance actually gains by having more.
11.notes:
The NLT translates the final line differently: “So what good is wealth — except perhaps to watch it slip through your fingers!” The NKJV pictures the owner looking at goods he still has, while the NLT pictures him watching them disappear. In both versions, all the owner gets is what his eyes take in.

The word “profit” links this verse to verse 9 just before it and to verse 16, where the question returns at the close of the next example: “And what profit has he who has labored for the wind?” All three echo the book’s opening question in 1:3.

12.brief: The laboring man sleeps sweetly whether he has eaten little or much, while the rich man's abundance keeps him awake. Wealth that seems to promise security often brings worry instead. The verse describes a common pattern; it does not say that every sleepless night comes from greed.
12.explain:
The sleep of a laboring man is sweet introduces an ordinary worker who is never described as wealthy. His sleep is “sweet,” restful and satisfying at the end of a day’s work. The contrast with verse 11 is deliberate. The owner gained little from his goods except the sight of them, but the laborer has something the owner’s wealth cannot buy.

Whether he eats little or much shows that the worker’s rest does not depend on how full his table is. Even on lean days he sleeps well. This picks up the language of eating from verse 11. There, other people consume the rich man’s goods. Here, the worker’s small or large meal makes no difference to his peace.

But the abundance of the rich will not permit him to sleep completes the contrast. Abundance could not satisfy its lover in verse 10, and here it robs the rich man of rest. Wealth that seems to promise security brings worry instead: concern for the goods, the claims of everyone who lives from them, and the danger of losing them, which verses 13–14 go on to describe. Solomon is describing a common pattern, not a rule for every case. He does not say that every rich person lies awake, that every sleepless night comes from greed, or that poverty is good in itself.
12.notes:
The NLT reads, “But the rich seldom get a good night’s sleep.” The word “seldom” presents the observation as a general tendency. The NKJV’s “will not permit him to sleep” describes the rich man in this picture more absolutely.

Solomon described sleepless toil earlier, in 2:23, where the worker’s days are sorrowful and “even in the night his heart takes no rest.” There, the burden of labor keeps him awake. Here, the burden of abundance does.

The language of eating runs through the rest of the chapter: “They increase who eat them” (verse 11), “Whether he eats little or much” (verse 12), “All his days he also eats in darkness” (verse 17), “to eat and drink” (verse 18), and “power to eat of it” (verse 19). The repeated word sets the restless owner and the man who eats in darkness against the person who eats as God’s gift.

13.brief: With the formal words “There is a severe evil which I have seen under the sun,” Solomon begins a single extended example: riches kept by their owner end up harming him. The wealth he held onto for his own good turns against him.
13.explain:
There is a severe evil which I have seen under the sun: After the short sayings about money in verses 10–12, Solomon slows down to tell one case he has watched with his own eyes. He calls it “a severe evil” because the outcome is grievous and hard to bear. The riches themselves are not called wicked; what is evil is the painful way this man’s life turns out. The phrase “under the sun” places the case inside Solomon’s examination of life measured only by earthly gain and the grave. Within that horizon, the story he is about to tell has no happy ending.

Riches kept for their owner to his hurt. The man has wealth, and he guards it, holding it back for his own benefit. Yet the very riches he keeps for his good become the source of his harm. Solomon does not yet say how the harm comes; the following verses tell it: the riches are lost, the son inherits nothing, the man leaves the world with empty hands, and his days fill with gloom. Verse 12 has already hinted at the problem, since “the abundance of the rich will not permit him to sleep.” The irony is sharp. Keeping wealth was supposed to make him secure, and keeping it is what hurt him. Solomon is describing what happened in this case, not saying that every person who owns or saves money comes to harm.
13.notes:
The opening words of this verse are echoed in verse 16, “And this also is a severe evil,” and the two statements frame a single case running through verses 13–16. A similar introduction returns at 6:1, “There is an evil which I have seen under the sun,” where Solomon describes a man to whom God gives riches but “does not give him power to eat of it” (6:2).

The NLT renders the second line “Hoarding riches harms the saver,” reading “kept” as hoarding and “his hurt” as harm to the one who saves. The NKJV’s “kept for their owner” states the same idea more generally.

14.brief: The stored-up riches are then lost through some misfortune, so when the man has a son there is “nothing in his hand” to give him. All his saving ends in empty hands, and the next generation inherits nothing.
14.explain:
But those riches perish through misfortune; The wealth the man guarded so carefully simply vanishes. Solomon says the riches “perish,” as though they die, and he does not name the cause. “Misfortune” covers any turn of events that wipes out what a person has built. The point is that wealth held for security proves to be insecure. Solomon calls the loss misfortune; he does not present it as God’s punishment for greed, and the verse gives no ground for treating every financial loss that way.

When he begets a son, there is nothing in his hand. Then a son is born, and the man has nothing to give him. A father who saves often hopes to leave something to his children, and that hope makes the loss more painful. Back in 2:18–19 Solomon grieved that he must leave his labor to someone who might be a fool. This man does not even have that problem, because nothing is left to pass on. All his saving ends in an empty hand, and the next generation receives nothing from it.
14.notes:
The NKJV wording “there is nothing in his hand” can be read as the father having nothing to hand on or as the son receiving nothing. Either way, the next generation is left with nothing. The NLT’s “nothing left to pass on to one’s children” describes it from the father’s side.

The NLT’s “risky investments that turn sour” gives one specific picture of how the riches were lost. The NKJV’s “misfortune” leaves the cause unnamed, which keeps the example open to many kinds of loss.

15.brief: The example now becomes a truth for everyone: just as a person came from the womb “naked,” he will go the same way at death, carrying nothing from his labor in his hand. Because death strips away every possession, wealth can never be lasting gain.
15.explain:
As he came from his mother’s womb, naked shall he return, Solomon now moves from one man’s bad luck to something true of every person. Each of us entered the world with nothing, not even clothing. To “return” naked means to leave life in the same condition, owning nothing. Death brings a person back to where he started.

To go as he came; The short line repeats the thought so that it cannot be missed: the way out of life matches the way in. Riches gathered in between change nothing about either end.

And he shall take nothing from his labor Which he may carry away in his hand. Even if this man’s riches had never been lost, death would have taken them from him anyway. His labor produced nothing he can carry past the grave. That is why wealth can never be the lasting gain people hope for, and it prepares for the question about “profit” in the next verse.
15.notes:
The word “hand” links verses 14 and 15. The man has “nothing in his hand” for his son, and at death he can take nothing from his labor “which he may carry away in his hand.” The father who could hand nothing on is himself carried out with nothing, so both generations end empty-handed.

The NKJV keeps the singular “he,” carrying forward the man of verses 13–14 while stating something true of every person. The NLT switches to “We all” and “We can’t take our riches with us,” which states that general truth openly.

16.brief: Solomon calls this “a severe evil” as well, closing the example he began in verse 13: a person leaves this world exactly as he came. His question, “what profit has he who has labored for the wind?” shows that labor spent only on gaining and keeping riches leaves nothing behind.
16.explain:
And this also is a severe evil— Solomon uses the same label he used in verse 13, which rounds off the case. The word “also” adds a second grievous fact to the first. Losing one’s riches is painful enough, but even a person who keeps his wealth to the end must leave without it.

Just exactly as he came, so shall he go. This is the third time in two verses that Solomon says the same thing. “Just exactly” allows no exceptions: wealth cannot buy a different way out of life.

And what profit has he who has labored for the wind? The question echoes the one that opens the book: “What profit has a man from all his labor In which he toils under the sun?” (1:3). “Profit” means the lasting gain left over after a lifetime of work. To labor “for the wind” is to work for something no one can catch or keep. The expected answer is that there is no profit at all. The question is aimed at labor spent only on gaining and keeping riches. Solomon is not calling all work worthless, because in verse 18 he commends enjoying one’s labor as God’s gift.
16.notes:
The phrase “labored for the wind” is close to the book’s recurring phrase “grasping for the wind” (found in verses from 1:14 to 6:9) but is not the same wording, and “grasping for the wind” does not occur here. Both picture effort aimed at something that cannot be held. The NLT renders this line “like working for the wind.”

“Profit” is a repeated word in this chapter. Verse 9 says “the profit of the land is for all.” Verse 11 asks “what profit have the owners Except to see them with their eyes?” Here, at death, the man does not have even that much: there is nothing left to look at.

17.brief: The man who labored for the wind eats all his days “in darkness” and carries “much sorrow and sickness and anger.” The emptiness of his pursuit does not wait for death; it spreads gloom and bitterness over ordinary daily life now.
17.explain:
All his days he also eats in darkness, The cost of laboring for the wind is not paid only at the end. Through “all his days” this man sits down to the most ordinary act, eating a meal, and does it “in darkness.” Eating should be a time of refreshment and gladness. For him it is shadowed by gloom. The image prepares for the contrast in the next verse, where Solomon commends eating and drinking “all the days of his life which God gives him.” God is not named anywhere from verse 8 through verse 17. When He reappears in verse 18, He comes as the Giver, and the same daily meal becomes a gift instead of a gloomy routine.

And he has much sorrow and sickness and anger. Solomon lists what such a life produces. Sorrow is grief over what has been lost and cannot be kept. Sickness shows how the strain of the pursuit wears a person down. Anger is the frustration and resentment of someone who worked hard and has nothing to show for it. Each item is described as “much,” so this misery fills the days he is living now. Solomon is describing the man whose labor was spent on the wind. He does not say that every grieving, sick, or angry person must be a lover of money.
17.notes:
Solomon described the same pattern in his own search: “For all his days are sorrowful, and his work burdensome; even in the night his heart takes no rest” (2:23). In both places sorrow and restlessness follow labor whose results must be left behind (2:18–23). Within this chapter, verse 12 has already pictured the rich man unable to sleep.

The NLT’s “they live under a cloud — frustrated, discouraged, and angry” turns the NKJV’s “eats in darkness” into a modern image and does not keep either the picture of eating or the word “sickness.” The NKJV’s eating image is worth noticing, because verse 18 commends the same act of eating and drinking as part of life received from God.

18.brief: Against that empty pursuit Solomon sets what he has seen to be “good and fitting”: to eat, drink, and enjoy the good of one's labor through all the days “which God gives him,” because this is one's “heritage.” This is genuine counsel within the book, and here “under the sun” simply places that enjoyment in life on earth.
18.explain:
Here is what I have seen: Solomon opens his counsel with the same kind of first-hand report he used in verse 13, where he described “a severe evil which I have seen under the sun.” That earlier sight was riches hoarded, lost, and leaving nothing behind. Now he reports something he has seen to be good. Placing the two observations side by side invites the reader to compare a life spent clutching wealth with a life that receives what God gives.

It is good and fitting for one to eat and drink, Only one verse earlier, the man who “labored for the wind” was said to eat “in darkness” all his days (verse 17). Solomon now commends the very same ordinary act. Eating and drinking are called “good,” something of real worth, and “fitting,” something that properly belongs to human life. The meal itself was never the problem. What separates the two lives is the way the same daily bread is received.

and to enjoy the good of all his labor in which he toils under the sun Solomon does not pretend that work is easy. It is still labor in which a person “toils.” Yet the work that left the hoarder with empty hands can yield good that is actually tasted and enjoyed along the way. Here the phrase “under the sun” does not mark another mistaken conclusion in Solomon’s search. It simply places this enjoyment in ordinary life on earth, where people work, eat, and live out their days.

all the days of his life which God gives him; God has not been named since verse 7, while Solomon described oppressive officials, restless money, and lost riches. Now He returns as the Giver. The days themselves are His gift, and the wording quietly admits that they are limited in number. A person does not own his lifetime or produce it by effort; he receives it one day at a time from God.

for it is his heritage. A heritage is the share assigned to someone, the portion that is his to receive. Solomon calls this enjoyment of food, drink, and work a person’s God-given portion in life. It is something received from God’s hand, not seized or manufactured. That stands in sharp contrast to the hoarder of verse 14, whose riches perished so that there was “nothing in his hand” for his son.
18.notes:
Within this chapter the phrase “under the sun” appears only twice, in verse 13 and here in verse 18. It frames both the “severe evil” of riches lost and the good of enjoyment received from God, so the same earthly setting holds both outcomes.

The NLT renders “all the days of his life which God gives him” as “during the short life God has given them,” making explicit the brevity that verse 20 addresses. It also renders “it is his heritage” as “to accept their lot in life,” bringing out the sense of a share assigned to a person.

Almost the same wording returns in 8:15, where Solomon commends eating, drinking, and being merry “all the days of his life which God gives him under the sun.” The repetition ties the two enjoyment passages together.

19.brief: Solomon names two distinct gifts: God gives riches and wealth, and He also gives the “power to eat of it,” to receive one's heritage and rejoice in one's labor. Both the possessions and the ability to enjoy them are “the gift of God,” so wealth is neither evil in itself nor a measure of God's approval. The difference between having and enjoying returns in 6:1–2, where Solomon describes a man to whom God gives riches but not that power.
19.explain:
As for every man to whom God has given riches and wealth, Solomon names God as the source of wealth itself. After verses 10–17, a reader might conclude that money is simply a trap. Solomon closes that door: riches can come from God’s hand. At the same time, the words “every man to whom” describe those who have received wealth. They do not promise riches to everyone, and they do not make wealth a sign that God approves of the one who has it.

and given him power to eat of it, Here is a second, separate gift. To “eat of” wealth means to enjoy it and put it to good use in one’s own life. Having possessions and being able to enjoy them are two different things, and both depend on God. The man of verses 13–17 shows how wealth can end without that gift. By the close of his story his riches had harmed him and vanished, and he was eating in darkness, the opposite of the enjoyment this verse describes. Solomon does not say whether the man enjoyed his wealth for a while before he lost it.

to receive his heritage and rejoice in his labor— This phrase explains what the power to enjoy looks like. It means receiving one’s portion as a gift, picking up the word “heritage” from verse 18, and rejoicing in work rather than resenting it. The emphasis falls on receiving. Contentment begins when a person accepts what God has assigned instead of grasping endlessly for more, like the lover of silver in verse 10.

this is the gift of God. The long sentence gathers everything into one summary. The riches, the ability to enjoy them, the heritage, and the joy in labor all come from God. That is why wealth is neither evil in itself nor a measure of His favor: the decisive good is the Giver, and the power to enjoy is His to give or withhold. The next chapter opens with exactly that withholding, a man to whom God gives riches but not the power to enjoy them (6:1–2).
19.notes:
Ecclesiastes 6:2 repeats the key wording of this verse almost exactly: a man to whom God has given “riches and wealth and honor,” yet “God does not give him power to eat of it, but a foreigner consumes it.” The shared phrasing shows that 5:19 and 6:2 are meant to be read as a matched pair across the chapter break.

The NLT renders “power to eat of it” as “the good health to enjoy it.” Health is one way this power can be present or absent, but the NKJV wording is broader. The case in 6:2, where a stranger consumes the owner’s wealth, shows that the loss of enjoyment can come in other ways too.

The same phrase, “it is the gift of God,” appears in 3:13, where eating, drinking, and enjoying the good of one’s labor are likewise called God’s gift. In 2:24 Solomon said the same enjoyment was “from the hand of God.”

20.brief: The person who receives life as God's gift “will not dwell unduly on the days of his life,” because “God keeps him busy with the joy of his heart.” Joy from God keeps him from being consumed by how brief life is, without asking him to pretend that hardship is not real.
20.explain:
For he will not dwell unduly on the days of his life, The word “For” explains what happens to the person who has received God’s gift in verse 19. “The days of his life” picks up the same words from verse 18, where those days were called a gift from God and were limited in number. Such a person still knows his days are few. The difference is that he is not consumed by brooding over how quickly they pass. The word “unduly” matters here. Solomon is not commending a careless refusal to think about life’s brevity; he describes a person who is no longer gripped by it, unlike the man of verse 17 who lived in darkness, sorrow, and anger.

because God keeps him busy with the joy of his heart. God is the one acting in this clause. He fills the person’s attention with gladness, and that joy is located in “his heart,” an inward contentment that possessions alone could never supply. The joy is not a mask over hard realities, since this same chapter has spoken frankly about oppression, loss, and death. Joy from God keeps him from being consumed by how brief life is, without asking him to pretend hardship is not real. With this picture of a life occupied by God-given joy the chapter closes, just before 6:1–2 describes a man who has riches but lacks that gift.
20.notes: The exact force of “God keeps him busy” is less certain than the main point of the verse, and translations express it differently. The NLT reads “so busy enjoying life that they take no time to brood over the past,” which directs attention backward. The NKJV’s “the days of his life” leaves the time frame open and, in this context, recalls the limited days “which God gives him” in verse 18. Either way, the verse says that God-given joy keeps a person from being absorbed by life’s passing.
